<Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro, Rep. Lois Frankel>: True national security is not achieved through military force alone, nor through coercion, tariffs, or retreat from the world. It is built through sustained diplomacy, strategic development, humanitarian leadership, strong alliances, and the wise use of America's soft power.
The Fiscal Year 2027 National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations bill fails to meet that standard.
This bill should have been an opportunity for Congress to strengthen American leadership, protect our security, and advance our values. Instead, it reflects a dangerous retreat from the proven tools that help prevent conflict, stop disease, support stability, and save lives before crises reach our shores.
The bill was considered without a hearing with the Secretary of State and without sufficient assurance that funds already appropriated by Congress are being used as intended. At the same time, the Administration has hollowed out USAID, canceled programs, pushed out experienced personnel, and left a weakened State Department to assume responsibilities it was never designed or staffed to carry. This approach is not a strategy. It is a setup for failure.
Critical programs authorized and funded by Congress, including those supporting food security, basic education, access to clean water, and women's leadership, lack clear implementation plans. Cuts to family planning services have led to widespread clinic closures, depriving millions of individuals of essential care and contributing to increased health risks and preventable deaths.
The bill does nothing to address this lack of action. It compounds the problem by cutting humanitarian aid while crises are worsening across Africa, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East. It eliminates funding for UNFPA, reinstates and expands the Global Gag Rule, and undermines care for women and girls around the world. It zeroes out institutions such as the U.S. Institute of Peace, the Inter-American Foundation, and the U.S. African Development Foundation. It eliminates funding for the United Nations and UN Peacekeeping--at a time when global cooperation has never been more important.
These choices do not make America stronger. They weaken our influence, abandon our partners, and create openings for competitors like China to fill the vacuum. Democrats sought to address many of these deficiencies in both the bill and current Administration policy through amendments. However, most were rejected along party-line votes.
An amendment by Ranking Member Lois Frankel to restrict deportations to third countries without an individual's consent was rejected. Amendments to strike a $1 billion rescission of humanitarian funds offered by Ranking Member Rosa DeLauro; to remove harmful riders affecting women's health offered by Representative Grace Meng; to direct funding to support Ukraine offered by Representative Steny Hoyer; to require financial disclosures from Special Envoys and Representatives offered by Representative Norma Torres; to direct funds for reconstruction of civilian infrastructure in Gaza offered by Representative Mike Quigley; to require a GAO report on the impact of dismantling USAID offered by Representative Mark Pocan; and to strike harmful ideological riders, including new restrictions related to diversity and gender, offered by Representative Madeleine Dean were all similarly defeated on party-line votes.
The Committee did adopt two amendments: one offered by Representative Norma Torres to prohibit the removal of sanctions against individuals facing credible allegations of child trafficking, and another by Representative Adriano Espaillat affirming the sovereignty of Guyana.
Democrats support a strong military. But military strength alone cannot keep America safe. Diplomacy prevents wars before they begin. Global health programs stop outbreaks before they spread. Development reduces the desperation that fuels instability and extremism. Alliances ensure the United States does not face threats alone.
Taken together, this bill represents a retreat from American leadership at a time when global engagement is more necessary than ever. With an additional $2.7 billion cut in fiscal year 2027, funding for the programs and priorities under this bill has declined by $14 billion over the last four years. This means significantly less investment in diplomacy, development, and humanitarian assistance--while expenditures on military operations continue to rise.
This bill pulls back American leadership at exactly the wrong moment. It fails to reflect the bipartisan tradition of smart, forward-looking national security policy and fails to protect the tools that keep Americans safe. In short, it fails to meet the urgency of this moment.
For these reasons, Democrats opposed this bill and commit to working toward a bipartisan alternative that strengthens our alliances, restores effective development and humanitarian programs, protects women and girls, supports global health, and reflects the very best of American leadership.
Rosa DeLauro.
Lois Frankel.
